1.pericope_label: Now it came to pass in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, that Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the defenced cities of Judah ... and the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem
debates: The date of the campaign: Ellicott reports that the Assyrian inscriptions push it to the twenty-seventh year of the king of Judah and explains the received figure as an editorial reckoning, while one scholar he cites keeps the received sequence by lengthening the reign.
Whether the narrative keeps chronological order, since all the cities are said to be taken before an envoy is sent from a city still under siege.
outliers: Clarke holds that the parallel account in Kings and this one are two copies of a single narration whose differences are largely copyists’ mistakes, so that each corrects the other.
themes: The history as the seal of the prophecy
Trouble meeting a people in the way of their duty
The embassy and the threatened water supply

4.pericope_label: Thus saith the great king, the king of Assyria, What confidence is this wherein thou trustest? ... thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt ... but if thou say to me, We trust in the Lord our God
debates: What the word of the lips means: Gill reports a reading that makes it prayer, on Kimchi’s authority, and another that makes it the king’s eloquence; Calvin rejects the first as far-fetched and takes the second.
Whether the charge of trusting Egypt is true: Calvin holds it a slander against the king personally, while granting that the people had earned the reproach.
outliers: Clarke reports fourteen manuscripts and the parallel copy putting the opening verb in the second person, and two ancient manuscripts with three versions giving a plural in the last verse.
themes: The summons of the great king
The broken reed of Egypt
The reformation turned into an accusation

8.pericope_label: Now therefore give pledges to my master the king of Assyria, and I will give thee two thousand horses ... am I now come up without the Lord against this land to destroy it?
debates: Whether the opening means give pledges or make a wager: Gill keeps the pledges and offers three senses, Ellicott reads a wager interpolated into the official message, Calvin reads the whole offer as irony.
Where the claim of a divine commission comes from: Clarke supposes an apostate priest suggested it, Ellicott offers an empty boast, a leaked prophecy, or a claimed dream.
outliers: Gill rejects the reading that makes the envoy speak of himself as the least of the captains, on the ground that so imperious a speaker would not.
themes: The jeer at a kingdom without cavalry
A commission claimed in God’s name
Slander borne by an upright conscience

11.pericope_label: Then said Eliakim ... Speak, I pray thee, unto thy servants in the Syrian language ... but Rabshakeh said, Hath my master sent me to thy master and to thee to speak these words? ... then Rabshakeh stood, and cried with a loud voice in the Jews language
debates: What the Jews language means: Ellicott weighs simple Hebrew, which the prophet elsewhere calls the language of Canaan, against a dialect of Judah, and finds the narrower sense elsewhere only after the exile.
outliers: Clarke reports an old version reading a negative, that they may not eat, and thinks it perhaps right; a large body of manuscripts substitutes the water, with a modest marginal circumlocution.
Ellicott finds the coarseness of the reply almost without parallel in history until a statesman of his own century.
themes: A king humbled to entreaty
An appeal over the rulers heads to the people
The holy tongue turned to blasphemy

14.pericope_label: Thus saith the king, Let not Hezekiah deceive you ... make an agreement with me by a present, and come out to me ... until I come and take you away to a land like your own land
debates: What land is promised: Gill reports one opinion naming a region resembling Judea and another naming Africa, and answers that no land was named because none could be named like Canaan.
outliers: Clarke reads the word for agreement as a blessing, that is a ransom for the city and the yearly tribute already promised; Calvin takes it figuratively for a present and reports an old version rendering it simply as making peace.
Clarke notes that the parallel copy adds a clause about a land of oil-olive and of honey.
themes: Trust in God attacked as imposture
A certain good offered against an unseen hope
Banishment veiled as a fertile land

18.pericope_label: Beware lest Hezekiah persuade you ... hath any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arphad?
debates: How the closing clause should be pointed: Calvin declines to make it a question and reads it as irony, that your God should deliver you as the gods of the nations delivered theirs.

Whether the speaker is merely exposing the weakness of idols: Ellicott takes him to be speaking the ordinary language of polytheism, Calvin holds that in the idols he pours contempt on the power of God himself.
outliers: Ellicott answers the taunt from the practice of the invaders: the gods of the fallen cities were to be seen in the temples of Assyria as trophies.
Clarke reports many manuscripts adding a conjunction, two further names in the parallel copy, and a conjecture reading the copulative as an interrogative particle.
themes: Blasphemy that levels God with the idols
Conquest mistaken for superiority over God
The rod that thought not so

21.pericope_label: But they held their peace, and answered him not a word: for the king’s commandment was, saying, Answer him not. Then came Eliakim ... to Hezekiah with their clothes rent, and told him the words of Rabshakeh
debates: Who held their peace: Clarke reports that the people is supplied from the parallel copy, and Calvin decides for the men on the wall rather than the ambassadors.

Whether silence under blasphemy can be justified: Calvin puts the objection against himself and answers that the silence was not consent, since the torn garments testified what no words could safely say.
outliers: Calvin excepts one of the three from the sincerity of the mourning, judging him destitute of piety and moved only by shame.
Calvin attributes the custom of rending garments to the warmer temperament of eastern nations, contrasted with the inhabitants of cold countries.
themes: Silence commanded and obeyed
A protest made without words
Zeal measured by what offends us
